newsitem.title: USA: Curtis says no talk with Clinton on top Energy job.
newsitem.headline: Curtis says no talk with Clinton on top Energy job.

text.p: Deputy U.S. Energy Secretary Charles Curtis Tuesday said he has not talked with President Clinton about assuming the Energy Department's top job, but declined to say whether he had spoken with other White House officials on the matter.
"I've had no discussions with the president about this subject and he's the only one who counts," Curtis told reporters while attending the American Petroleum Institute's annual meeting.
But Curtis declined to comment on whether he had talked with anyone else at the White House.
Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary plans to leave, her spokeswoman has said, and Curtis is among several mentioned by industry and congressional sources as a potential replacement.
"I think speculation that the cabinet will take form by the end of the year is right," Curtis said.
On other matters in remarks at the API meeting, Curtis said he expected pressure will continue to sell Strategic Petroleum Reserve oil to help balance the budget.
He also said that he doubted the ban on oil drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Reserve or existing offshore drilling moratoria would be lifted in this Congress.

"There is no question that the Strategic Petroleum Reserve is going be part of the mix" when Congress and the White House discuss a balanced budget plan, Curtis said. "The question will remain how it will come out of that mix," he said.
"There's an irresistible temptation to reach to that oil as a source for deficit reduction. What we really have to look to is in the out-term long-range budget plan," he said.
But Curtis said under the law, it is difficult for the president to draw the reserve below 580 million barrels.

On drilling in Alaska's Arctic National Wildlife Reserve, a move pushed repeatedly by Alaska's congressmen, Curtis said: "The question of opening ANWR prdocution is a matter that was settled in the first Clinton Administration. I do not see it being reopened. I don't believe it will change."

On keeping offshore drilling moratoria, he said: "The moratorium issue is one of the more politically-sensitive issues in the congress. I think the moratoria that are in effect are likely to remain in effect for the duration of the next Congress. I don't think anyone in the administration or the Congress is ready to take that on."
Curtis also said he was leery of using sanctions against other countries.
"I am not a believer in sanctions," he said, adding that he believed the United States should remain engaged in other countries' economies.
"As a general principle I will always try to raise a very high bar" when sanctions are proposed, Curtis said. "We must continually test both the effectivness and rationale behind sanctions policy."
Curtis also called on the oil industry to help secure funding for research on global climate change caused by burning fossil fuels.
While the United States is the largest supporter of the research, he said, "That program is under severe funding constraints."

"You can help secure funding for us. You can help us refine and ensure the relevance of our research programs," he told the oil industry gathering, adding that he expected the Energy Department's "science and information capabilities will have an even greater role in the next administration."
